meta.note: Every source in this library was read and analyzed — not merely listed. Official ASEAN documents, academic papers, policy reports, bilateral programme records, and a 14-dimension research synthesis. Each entry carries what we took from it.

entries.title: ASCN Concept Note
entries.takeaway: Establishes the network as a cooperative platform with three objectives: facilitate cooperation, catalyse bankable projects, secure external-partner funding. The 'people-first, technology-as-enabler' frame originates here — technology serves human outcomes, not the reverse.

entries.title: ASEAN Smart Cities Framework
entries.takeaway: The non-binding guide: three strategic outcomes, two urban systems, six focus areas, two enablers. Deliberately a guide, not a mandate — the structural reason ASCN coordinates rather than commands. Its voluntary nature is both its strength (inclusivity) and its weakness (no enforcement).

entries.title: East Asia Summit Leaders' Statement on ASEAN Smart Cities
entries.takeaway: Heads of State of ASEAN plus Australia, China, India, Japan, Korea, New Zealand, Russia and the US endorsed the network on 15 November 2018 — the political basis for the eight-partner cooperation ecosystem. This multi-power endorsement explains why ASCN has avoided becoming a bilateral arrangement dominated by any single external partner.

entries.title: Consolidated Smart City Action Plans (SCAPs)
entries.takeaway: The priority areas and action plans of the 26 pilot cities, self-defined by each city — the original source of the project portfolio and its locally-owned, uneven character. Reading these reveals that cities prioritised civic services and infrastructure over technology for its own sake.

entries.title: ASCN Terms of Reference & M&E Framework — Bangkok adoption
entries.takeaway: The 22–24 August 2019 meeting at CentralWorld Bangkok where the ASCN Terms of Reference and the Monitoring & Evaluation Framework were formally adopted — the procedural birth of the annual reporting cycle this platform reads. Thailand chaired this session as ASCN chair.

entries.title: ASCN M&E Report 2022
entries.takeaway: The baseline M&E cycle: a 77-project portfolio across the roster, the first consolidated read of network-wide implementation. Confirms the method counts project outputs (status: ongoing/completed/planning), not citizen outcomes — a structural gap that all subsequent cycles inherit.

entries.title: ASCN M&E Report 2023
entries.takeaway: Second M&E cycle — roster and portfolio growth; investment framing sharpens under Indonesia's shepherdship. Cambodia's Green Smart City theme is visible in new environmental projects. Total grows toward 108 projects.

entries.title: ASCN M&E Report 2024
entries.takeaway: Portfolio reaches 108 projects; the financing toolkit and ASUF activity mature. Go! Manila reports 1.2 million registrants and 15.9 billion pesos in collection — the clearest documented citizen-scale impact in any M&E cycle to date.

entries.title: ASCN M&E Report 2025 (as of 30 Sep 2025)
entries.takeaway: 134 projects, 81% ongoing — the primary appendix source for this platform's project database. Dottoro'ta (Makassar) has now attended 6,973+ patients; JakPreneur (Jakarta) has 405,052 MSME registrants. The report confirms the M&E method still counts projects, not outcomes. Timor-Leste's Dili appears for the first time.

entries.title: ASEAN Smart City Planning Guidebook
entries.takeaway: The shared planning methodology offered to member cities — useful as a baseline, but a single template applied across radically different cities from Singapore to Luang Prabang. Useful for its city-engagement examples: Jakarta uses Instagram/YouTube, Cebu uses public meetings, Bandar Seri Begawan uses mobile citizen reporting.

entries.title: ASCN under Singapore's Chairmanship
entries.takeaway: Founding-year activities and the handover into the Shepherd model — Singapore's institutional design for surviving annual chair rotation. Singapore explicitly designed ASCN's architecture (the Framework, the CLC knowledge partnership) before handing the chair forward, ensuring continuity through design rather than through power.

entries.title: ASCN 2019: Advancing Partnership for Sustainability
entries.source: DEPA / Ministry of Digital Economy and Society, Thailand
entries.takeaway: Thailand's chairmanship-year report, edited by DEPA leadership — the clearest record of Thailand's organising role and the partnership-for-sustainability theme. Thailand hosted the TOR/M&E adoption, convened the Annual Meeting in Bangkok, and co-produced the first ASCN external-partnership framework.

entries.title: ASCN 2019 Report (rev.02)
entries.takeaway: The detailed editorial record of the Thai chair year — confirms Thailand's early, hands-on stewardship of the network's operational machinery. The revision (rev.02) corrects several project counts from the initial publication, signaling early attention to data accuracy.

entries.title: Cabinet Resolution on the ASCN Progress Report (มติ ครม. 29 ต.ค. 2562)
entries.takeaway: ASCN reporting reached Thailand's Cabinet on 29 October 2019 — evidence the network was treated as national policy, not a side initiative. This cabinet-level engagement is the institutional basis for Thailand's continuing leadership: DEPA has the mandate, the PM Office has seen the reports.

entries.title: ASCN Contact List (as of 31 Jan 2026)
entries.takeaway: National focal points and city representatives across all 38 cities — the human network behind the roster. Personal contact details are withheld from public display here, but the document confirms that every city has a designated representative who carries the city's participation between annual meetings.

entries.title: MLIT ASEAN Smart City Planning Guidebook (Draft Final)
entries.takeaway: Japan's draft methodology submitted for ASCN consideration — a case study in how a partner's planning framework becomes regional practice. Its urban-spatial emphasis reflects Japanese city planning tradition; the risk is template transfer without local adaptation.

entries.title: Smart City Handbook: Thailand
entries.takeaway: DEPA's national smart city playbook — the most developed of any ASCN member, including the Thai Smart City Index that already does the outcome-level measurement the regional M&E lacks. Thailand's index covers economy, mobility, environment, energy, ICT, and people — a parallel system that proves the regional gap is solvable.

entries.title: Smart City Week 2020 — Proceedings (EN)
entries.takeaway: Thailand's flagship convening of regional smart-city practice — demonstrates a model built on open exchange and showcase rather than vendor lock-in. The bilingual proceedings signal Thai capacity to host peer learning for the region, not merely consume it.

entries.title: Smart City Week 2020 — Proceedings (TH)
entries.takeaway: The Thai-language edition — evidence the work is built for its own public first, in its own language, not translated in from outside. This matters: the best national smart city programmes are understood by their own citizens before they are exported.

entries.title: Case Study of the ASEAN Smart Cities Network
entries.takeaway: The landmark policy-transfer study of ASCN, based on 19 key informant interviews. Identifies five structural barriers to transboundary learning: lack of political will, multi-level bureaucracy, fiscal constraints, insufficient policy capacity, and lack of operational/regulatory mechanisms. Singapore's architect role in designing the network is documented here.

entries.title: Human Rights and the ASEAN Smart Cities Network
entries.takeaway: The most direct critical analysis: ASCN risks marginalizing vulnerable communities in technocratic planning; technology introduction may increase surveillance and control in less democratic ASEAN settings. A dissenting peer reviewer found the argument one-sided — both views matter for a balanced read of the evidence.

entries.title: Indonesia's Smart City Diplomacy Through ASCN Shepherdship (2023–2025)
entries.source: Prayogo & Juned — Journal of Social and Political Sciences
entries.takeaway: Documents Indonesia's pivot from Singapore's conceptual approach to pragmatic implementation, with the ASEAN Smart City Investment Toolkit as the principal legacy. The insight: where Singapore built the architecture, Indonesia built the engine — different kinds of leadership, both necessary.

entries.title: SMART CITY IN ASEAN: A Systematic Review
entries.source: Hati & Kartikasari — Revista de Gestão Social e Ambiental
entries.takeaway: Bibliometric analysis of 156 full-text Scopus-indexed articles on ASEAN smart cities. Reveals convergence between capitalist and eco-culturalist approaches, and significant gaps in cybersecurity frameworks and data privacy protection. Useful as the map of what scholarship has and hasn't studied.

entries.title: Assessing the ASEAN Smart Cities Network (Quintuple Helix Framework)
entries.source: Crumpton et al. — International Journal of Urban Sustainable Development
entries.takeaway: Applies the Quintuple Helix Innovation Framework to assess ASCN, finding deficiencies in civil participation and environmental performance. The framework (academic + industry + government + civil society + natural environment) is a useful lens because it makes the civil society gap visible — a gap ASCN's top-down model consistently produces.

entries.title: Scaling smartness, (de)provincialising the city?
entries.takeaway: Analyses 'technocratic regionalism' in ASCN — the way a Singapore-led technical network can inadvertently position Asian cities as recipients of smart-city concepts rather than originators. The relevance of this article to Thailand's role is direct: Thailand's own index and methodology challenges this framing by originating its own framework.

entries.title: ASCN Cooperation for Digital Inclusion: Indonesia and Malaysia
entries.takeaway: Comparative study of Indonesia and Malaysia's ASCN implementation: Indonesia focuses on MSME empowerment and digital public services; Malaysia emphasises urban data management and transport. Only 55% of ASEAN population has internet access — this figure anchors the inclusion gap that both implementations must navigate.

entries.title: South-South Cooperation and the Promise of Experimentalist Governance in ASCN
entries.takeaway: 'Experimentalist governance without diagnostic monitoring' — the sharpest scholarly characterisation of ASCN's structural problem. The network runs experiments (projects) but cannot diagnose which experiments work because outcome measurement is absent. This framing directly motivates the platform's M&E critique.

entries.title: Gender equality in smart sustainable cities
entries.takeaway: Jakarta's multimodal public transport evaluation from a gender perspective reveals service gaps and differences in satisfaction between genders. Documents that gender-based service analysis exists and produces actionable findings — evidence that GESI approaches in ASCN cities can generate real design improvements.

entries.title: ASEAN-Australia Smart Cities Trust Fund Mid-Term Review
entries.takeaway: AUD 20 million programme across 24 cities in 8 countries. Key finding: strong GESI intentions (Gender Equality and Social Inclusion) but 'no tangible evidence yet of benefits to GESI target groups.' The Makassar Dottoro'ta and Baguio FEWS projects are documented as best-practice inclusions. Detailed task-order funding table available.

entries.title: Smart City Pathways for Developing Asia
entries.takeaway: ADB's conceptual foundation for smart city financing in the region, introducing the ASEAN Smart Cities Initiative as a co-operating framework. Identifies three ASEAN urban priorities: mobility, basic infrastructure, integrated development. Sets the scene for why the ACGF and AASCTF took the forms they did.

entries.title: Asia-Pacific Regional Guidelines for Smart Cities
entries.takeaway: The most recent UN-level guidelines for smart city practice in the Asia-Pacific. Emphasises that smart cities must not exclude 'marginalized communities, girls, women, and persons with disabilities.' Specifies including informal settlement residents in water management design — a standard that ASCN's current top-down model does not systematically meet.

entries.title: Survey for Framework Building of People-Centric Smart City Model
entries.takeaway: Thailand's KPI framework for smart city development sets a target of 70% of citizens gaining Digital Literacy Skills annually — the most specific outcome KPI in any ASCN member's national framework. ERIA's role as ASEAN's economic research think tank gives this framework regional legitimacy.

entries.title: Mapping the Landscape of Smart Cities in the Philippines
entries.takeaway: 72% of Philippine LGUs allocated funding for smart city projects; 67% identified lack of funding as the top challenge. The paradox is precise: cities fund smart city work from existing budgets while simultaneously saying they lack funds — evidence that smart city projects are competing with basic services rather than complementing them.

entries.title: Enabling Inclusion in Smart City Development: A Policy Toolkit
entries.takeaway: Uses ASCN Action Plans as case studies to document exclusion risks: institutional structures concentrating power, informal workforce displacement through automation, urban rejuvenation displacing low-income communities. The Khon Kaen community leader quote ('Only the rich can benefit') is in this document. Essential companion to any ASCN inclusion claim.

entries.title: ASEAN Smart City Financing Toolkit
entries.takeaway: Launched November 2024 in Jakarta, providing guidance on financing options for smart city projects across the ASCN. Represents the convergence of ADB, bilateral partners, and the ACGF blended-finance approach into a single reference. Indonesia's shepherdship legacy — the shift from concept to capital.

entries.title: AIIB Sustainable Cities Strategy and Study
entries.takeaway: AIIB's 288 projects totalling USD 55.34 billion as of November 2024 position it as a significant co-financer for ASEAN urban infrastructure. Its ability to finance both sovereign and sub-national entities directly makes it relevant to ASCN cities that need project-level rather than national-level loans.

entries.title: Third ASEAN Web Forum on Disability-Inclusion, Smart Cities and Connectivity
entries.takeaway: ASEAN Deputy Secretary-General called for universal design at the heart of smart city expansion. Five recommendations issued: promote universal design, advance data and research, strengthen collaboration including persons with disabilities, create supportive financing, foster accessibility audits in M&E. None of these five recommendations appear in the 2025 M&E Report's standard metrics.

entries.title: ASEAN Foundation Digital Literacy Programmes
entries.takeaway: 200,000+ individuals trained across all ASEAN Member States through the ASEAN Digital Literacy Programme and ASEAN Cybersecurity Skilling Programme. The master-trainer model with private sector involvement is scalable — but the Tech for Good Institute notes that 'reach' (learners trained) is still not the same as 'proficiency' (skills acquired).

entries.title: ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA)
entries.takeaway: Signed October 2025, DEFA covers cross-border data flows, AI governance, and cybersecurity. Combined with ASCAP 2026-2035, creates a rare policy window to establish common smart city data standards before vendor lock-in solidifies. The two frameworks converging in 2025-2026 is the most significant institutional development since ASCN's founding.

entries.title: IMD Smart City Index 2025
entries.takeaway: Singapore scores 81 on smart city accessibility (2nd globally) with fully accessible subway, braille guidance, and 95% of sidewalks/crossings adapted for disability access. The contrast with most other ASCN cities — where accessibility data is absent from M&E reporting — is the measurement gap in microcosm.

entries.title: ASCN City-Level Open Data Platforms
entries.takeaway: Six documented open data platforms: KLUO (Kuala Lumpur Urban Observatory), IMAC (Integrated Metropolitan Area Command, Makassar), SSDaP (Surabaya Smart Dashboard Platform), One Map Yangon, Manila's Go! app, Bangkok's Traffy Fondue. Each collects city-level data; none are interoperable. The data exists; cross-city aggregation does not.

entries.title: Dimension 01: Governance Structure and Political Dynamics
entries.takeaway: ASCN operates through the 'ASEAN Way' — voluntary, non-binding, consensus-based. The Chair-Shepherd model solves institutional continuity across annual rotation. Governance gaps: no enforcement mechanism, no binding outcome standards, no independent review body. Political will is variable by country and chair cycle.

entries.title: Dimension 02: Member Cities and Project Portfolio
entries.takeaway: Detailed analysis of all 38 cities and their project portfolios from four M&E cycles. Key finding: the portfolio is locally-owned but not locally-measured — cities define their own SCAPs but the network has no shared outcome metrics. Davao, Manila, Jakarta, Bangkok, and Makassar carry the heaviest documented project loads.

entries.title: Dimension 03: External Partnerships and Cooperation
entries.takeaway: Six major bilateral partners (Japan, Australia, EU, US, India, Korea) each run parallel tracks. Japan's SmartJAMP (JPY 250B) is the largest; Australia's AASCTF (AUD 20M) the most systematically documented. Coordination between partners is limited — each runs its own programme with minimal cross-partner learning.

entries.title: Dimension 04: Financing and Investment Landscape
entries.takeaway: No aggregated investment total exists — ASCN does not track cumulative financing. Documented projects range from USD 97K (Kaysone employment platform) to USD 1.074B (Davao PTMP). ADB is the dominant financier. Southeast Asia needs USD 7 trillion infrastructure investment by 2040; blended finance (ACGF, SmartJAMP) is converging toward this gap.

entries.title: Dimension 05: Monitoring, Evaluation, and Data Systems
entries.takeaway: The single most critical structural gap: ASCN counts projects (outputs) not citizen outcomes. Four M&E cycles produce consistent project tallies but no network-wide measure of whether smart cities improve lives. The fix is achievable — individual project narratives already contain outcome data; the problem is curation and standardisation.

entries.title: Dimension 06: Technology Architecture and Vendor Landscape
entries.takeaway: Huawei dominates in Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand; Ericsson in Singapore and Malaysia; Viettel (Vietnam's own 5G) is a notable exception. Vendor selection mirrors geopolitical alignments. Six separate city data platforms exist with no interoperability. DEFA 2025 creates the first regional data-governance framework that could address this fragmentation.

entries.title: Dimension 07: Transport and Mobility Projects
entries.takeaway: Transport is ASCN's largest focus area (~25% of projects) and has the most clearly quantified investment pipeline. Davao PTMP (USD 1.074B) is the network's largest single documented project; Bangkok Bang Sue (USD 6.7B) connects to ASCN through the national smart city framework. Transport is the most 'dashboard-ready' sector for investment tracking.

entries.title: Dimension 08: Environmental Performance and Climate Action
entries.takeaway: Environmental projects are Cambodia's thematic contribution under its 2022 chairmanship ('Green Smart City'). Quality Environment is the third-largest focus area (18%). Climate finance through ACGF (USD 300M GCF + USD 1.9B co-financing) is the largest single source of green investment in the network. Environmental outcome measurement is as absent as citizen outcome measurement.

entries.title: Dimension 09: Academic Research and Critical Analysis
entries.takeaway: Growing but modest scholarly literature since 2018. Key scholars: Taeihagh (NUS), Putra (Bristol), Prayogo (Indonesia), Crumpton. The dominant academic critique is experimentalist governance without diagnostic monitoring — ASCN runs experiments but cannot diagnose which work. Positive and critical scholarship both valuable; this platform represents neither endorsement nor critique.

entries.title: Dimension 10: Comparative Analysis with Peer Networks
entries.takeaway: ASCN compared to India's Smart Cities Mission (SCM), EU Cities Mission, US Smart Cities Council, C40, 100 Resilient Cities. The ASEAN Way model is unique: no dedicated fund, no binding targets, no scoring. EU's Climate City Contracts (binding commitments + EU funding) and India's SCM (top-down with SPVs) represent the opposite end. ASCN's voluntary model is more inclusive but less accountable.

entries.title: Dimension 11: Private Sector Engagement
entries.takeaway: Private sector engagement is more documented as technical assistance and equipment supply than as equity investment. Huawei, Siemens, Microsoft, Cisco are active in the ASEAN market, but direct documented investment in ASCN projects remains scarce. The risk of 'corporate visions of smartness' overriding social equity is a recurring concern in academic literature.

entries.title: Dimension 12: Citizen Impact, Digital Inclusion, and Social Equity
entries.takeaway: Impact data exists but is buried in project narratives: Go! Manila (1.2M registrants), JakPreneur (405K MSMEs), Dottoro'ta (6,973 patients), ASEAN Foundation (200K+ digital literacy trainees). The problem is curation, not absence of data. Digital divide persists: only 55% of ASEAN population has internet access.

entries.title: Dimension 13: Future Outlook and Strategic Scenarios
entries.takeaway: ASCAP 2026-2035 and DEFA 2025 create a 10-year window of unprecedented institutional alignment. Three scenarios: (1) data-platform convergence under DEFA — most optimistic; (2) continued fragmentation with national-level progress but no regional interoperability; (3) geopolitical vendor lock-in splits the network. Timor-Leste's inclusion forces ASCN to define 'smart city' for low-connectivity environments.

entries.title: Dimension 14: Data Sources and Open Data Infrastructure
entries.takeaway: A regional open data infrastructure does not exist: each city runs its own platform (KLUO, SSDaP, IMAC, Go! Manila) with no common schema. The ASCN M&E appendix is the closest to a network-level dataset, but it is PDF-locked in official reports. This platform's JSON exports are the first machine-readable version of the public record.

entries.title: ASCN Cross-Dimension Verification Report
entries.takeaway: 10 cross-cutting insights derived after reconciling all 14 dimensions: the M&E gap is the single biggest strategic vulnerability; financing is fragmented but converging; the ASEAN Way is both enabler and constraint; vendor geopolitics are real; Timor-Leste will test inclusivity; DEFA + ASCAP 2025-26 is a historic convergence window; citizen impact data exists but is hidden.

entries.title: City Statistics: Wikipedia/Wikidata/ASEAN merged dataset
entries.takeaway: Population, geographic coordinates, and administrative metadata for all 38 ASCN member cities, compiled from Wikipedia infoboxes, Wikidata, and ASEAN official records. Used to build the cities map and city profiles on this platform. Reveals significant data gaps: several cities lack reliable population figures in public sources.

entries.title: ASCN Comprehensive Research Brief (14-dimension, 500+ citations)
entries.takeaway: The synthesis spine of this platform — all 14 research dimensions integrated into a single brief covering governance, projects, partnerships, financing, M&E, technology, transport, environment, academic critique, comparative analysis, private sector, citizen impact, future outlook, and data sources. This is the backbone behind every claim on this site.

entries.title: Smart JAMP — Japan's USD 2.4 Billion ASEAN Smart City Initiative
entries.source: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) + JOIN
entries.takeaway: JPY 250 billion (USD 2.4B) fund comprising JPY 200B in JBIC loans and JPY 50B in JOIN equity, supporting Japanese companies in ASCN cities. Japan conducted feasibility studies in 26 ASCN cities across 10 sectors. The largest bilateral smart city commitment in the region — and largely invisible in the standard M&E reporting.

entries.title: ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility (ACGF)
entries.source: ASEAN Infrastructure Fund / ADB / Green Climate Fund
entries.takeaway: USD 300M from GCF + USD 1.9B co-financing pledges + USD 3.7B total project pipeline across 20 green infrastructure projects. The most significant blended finance mechanism in ASEAN and the template for how ASCN cities should access climate finance. The Davao PTMP's GCF component (USD 50M for electric buses) is funded through this facility.

entries.title: ASEAN Smart City Action Plan 2026–2035 (ASCAP)
entries.takeaway: Adopted September 2025, the 10-year action plan extends ASCN's mandate through 2035. Eight pillars of action covering digital governance, innovation ecosystems, climate, mobility, health, inclusive development, data infrastructure, and partnerships. Together with DEFA 2025, creates the most significant institutional alignment in ASCN's history.

entries.title: Davao Public Transport Modernization Project (DPTMP)
entries.source: Philippines DOTr / ADB / GCF / ASEAN Infrastructure Fund
entries.takeaway: USD 1.074B loan package — ADB's largest ever road-based public transport project in the Philippines and ASCN's single largest documented investment. 800,000 daily passengers, 1,105 buses across 29 routes, GCF co-financing for electric buses. The model for how ASCN connectivity leads to bankable project, multilateral financing, and citizen impact.
